summaries.example: Mia says, “Everyone in our class has a new game, so you should get one too.” This is an appeal to popularity. Lots of people liking something does not prove that it is best for everyone. We should ask for better reasons, such as whether the game is safe, useful, and affordable.
summaries.summary: A fallacy is a mistake in reasoning that can look better than it really is. The SEP entry explains two common ways people understand fallacies: as false beliefs that many people hold, or as bad arguments that appear persuasive. It focuses mainly on the second idea. Some fallacies use confusing language. For example, a word may quietly change meaning, or a sentence may be unclear. Other fallacies use reasons that do not properly support the conclusion. These include saying something is true because many people believe it, attacking a speaker instead of examining the claim, or deciding that one event caused another merely because it came first. A straw man changes a person’s real view into an easier view to defeat. A slippery slope claims that a small first step must lead through a chain of bad results, even when the links are not supported. The entry also describes a long history of studying fallacies, beginning with Aristotle and continuing through later writers. Modern philosophers disagree about whether fallacies are mainly logical mistakes, failures in knowledge, or rule-breaking in a discussion. They also debate whether a fallacy must seem correct to someone and whether memorizing a list is the best way to learn good reasoning.
key_ideas: Fallacies can make weak reasoning look convincing.
Some mistakes come from unclear words, while others come from irrelevant reasons or unsupported causes.
A person’s fame, popularity, or strong emotions do not automatically prove a claim.
Not every argument with a familiar fallacy name is bad in every situation; context matters.
Philosophers have disagreed about how fallacies should be defined and taught.
Learning about fallacies works best when combined with learning what makes a good argument.
summaries.why_it_matters: Fallacies appear in conversations, advertisements, school discussions, news, and online posts. Recognizing them can help you pause before accepting a claim or rejecting someone unfairly. The goal is not to label people, but to examine reasons carefully: Are the words clear? Is the evidence relevant? Does it really support the conclusion? Good reasoning also requires listening and being willing to change your mind when better evidence appears.

important_terms.definition: A piece of reasoning that seems strong or correct but has an important mistake.
A reason or group of reasons offered to support a conclusion.
A mistake caused by a word or sentence having more than one possible meaning.
Treating something as the cause of an event just because it happened earlier.
Using an unfair version of someone’s idea because it is easier to attack.
A reason based on what many people believe or do, instead of good evidence.

questions_to_think_about: Can a popular idea still be false?
How could you check whether one event really caused another?
Why is it unfair to change someone’s idea before arguing against it?

summaries.example: A student argues: “The new school rule must be harmful because its author was once suspended.” This is an abusive ad hominem if the author’s past behavior is offered as a reason to reject the rule itself. The author’s history might matter in assessing credibility in some contexts, but it does not by itself show that the rule is bad. The rule should be examined through its wording, evidence, effects, and justification.
summaries.summary: The SEP entry surveys fallacies as a contested subject in the theory of reasoning. A widely used working idea is that a fallacy is an argument that appears better than it is, but this formula contains several disputable conditions: it must be an argument, it must be defective, and it must have an appearance of correctness. The entry notes that popular speech often calls false or widely held beliefs “fallacies,” whereas scholarly treatments usually focus on defective arguments. It reviews the traditional core, including equivocation and amphiboly, mistakes involving parts and wholes, question-begging, complex questions, false-cause reasoning, irrelevant conclusions and straw man arguments, appeals to authority or popularity, threats and pity, ad hominem arguments, faulty analogy, and slippery slopes. These labels do not automatically settle an evaluation. An appeal to authority may be appropriate when the source is genuinely qualified and relevant; a threat may provide a practical reason to act, even though it is irrelevant evidence for believing a proposition. Likewise, an argument from analogy may be suggestive without being conclusive. Historically, Aristotle connected fallacies with apparent deductions and refutations. Later writers expanded attention to bias, ordinary discourse, induction, political debate, and arguments using ad-terms such as ad hominem and ad verecundiam. Contemporary theories diverge. Informal logic uses standards such as acceptability, relevance, and sufficiency. Epistemic theories ask whether premises can be justified independently of the conclusion. Dialectical theories examine whether moves violate rules of a reasonable dialogue. Other approaches use multiple logical systems, probability, or virtues of argumentation. The entry concludes that,
key_ideas: The entry distinguishes a belief conception of fallacies from an argument conception, and concentrates on arguments.

The traditional core includes ambiguity, composition and division, begging the question, irrelevant conclusion, causal errors, appeals to authority or popularity, ad hominem reasoning, faulty analogy, and slippery slopes.
Formal and informal fallacies are commonly distinguished, but informal fallacies are not one uniform category.
Begging the question is especially important because an argument may be logically valid yet fail to provide independent epistemic support.
Modern approaches evaluate fallacies through different ideals: logical validity, cogent support, epistemic justification, dialogue rules, or argumentation virtues.
Whether an argument is fallacious can depend on context, the goal of a dialogue, the evidence available, and the standards appropriate to the exchange.
summaries.why_it_matters: Fallacy theory matters because reasoning in natural language is richer than applying a small set of formal rules. A label can identify a possible problem, but responsible evaluation requires reconstructing the argument, identifying its purpose, checking its premises, and asking whether the inference is strong enough in context. This prevents two opposite errors: being persuaded by a deceptive argument and dismissing a good argument merely because it resembles a familiar fallacy. The debates also matter for education. important_terms.definition: A purported argument that falls short of a relevant standard of reasoning or argumentation; philosophers disagree about which standard is fundamental.
A deductively invalid pattern that can resemble a valid logical form.
A weakness in ordinary-language reasoning analyzed without relying mainly on symbolic logical form.
A word or expression is used with different meanings in different parts of an argument.
A sentence’s grammatical structure permits competing interpretations, affecting what the argument appears to say.
Assuming a conclusion, openly or in disguised form, instead of providing independent support for it.
Inferring causation merely from temporal order, or otherwise overlooking alternative causes.
A pattern of reasoning that can be reasonable in some contexts but weak or mistaken when its support fails critical questions.

questions_to_think_about: Should an appeal to an expert count as fallacious whenever experts disagree, or only when the chosen expert is irrelevant or unreliable?
Can a threat give someone a practical reason to act while still failing to give a reason to believe a claim?
Is the appearance of correctness necessary for calling an argument a fallacy?
Would teaching positive standards for good arguments be more useful than teaching a list of fallacy names?
How might bias explain why someone commits or accepts a fallacy?

summaries.example: Jordan says, “Our team won after I wore my lucky socks, so the socks caused the victory.” The argument may use false-cause reasoning. The win happened after the socks were put on, but that does not show the socks produced it. Practice, the other team’s mistakes, or chance might explain the result. The socks could be a fun tradition without being evidence of a cause.
summaries.summary: The SEP entry explains fallacies as a major topic in the study of reasoning. In everyday speech, people sometimes use “fallacy” for a popular but false belief. Philosophers more often study fallacies as arguments that seem persuasive even though they do not support their conclusions well. The traditional group includes language-based mistakes, such as equivocation, where a term changes meaning, and amphiboly, where grammar allows an argument to be read in different ways. Composition and division confuse the properties of parts with those of a whole. Begging the question gives the appearance of proof while assuming the point at issue. Other fallacies misdirect attention: a straw man replaces someone’s actual view with a weaker version, and an ad hominem attacks the speaker rather than the reasoning. Appeals to popularity, authority, pity, or threats may sometimes influence action, but they do not automatically provide evidence that a claim is true. Causal fallacies may treat sequence as proof of cause, ignore another cause, or confuse cause and effect. Faulty analogies rely on similarities that are too weak, while slippery-slope arguments do not adequately support the steps from a starting point to a feared outcome. The entry also presents the history of the subject. Aristotle analyzed apparent refutations; later writers considered bias, authority, induction, political argument, and ordinary language. Modern philosophers disagree about the best theory. Some focus on logical invalidity, some on whether premises are acceptable, relevant, and sufficient, some on independent justification, and some on rules for fair dialogue. key_ideas: A fallacy is often described as an argument that seems stronger than it really is, but philosophers disagree about whether this definition is complete.
Some fallacies depend on language, such as unclear grammar or a word changing meaning.
Other fallacies involve relevance, evidence, causation, authority, popularity, emotion, analogy, or the structure of a discussion.
A valid argument can still beg the question if its premises are not independently supported.
An argument can be reasonable in one setting and fallacious in another, depending on its goal and evidence.
The study of fallacies developed from Aristotle’s work and later included approaches focused on induction, everyday reasoning, dialogue, probability, and bias.
summaries.why_it_matters: Fallacies matter whenever people must decide what to believe or do. They can hide weak evidence behind popularity, confidence, emotion, or complicated wording. Studying them helps us ask better questions: What exactly is the conclusion? Which reasons support it? Are those reasons true or acceptable? Could another cause or explanation fit the evidence? Is the speaker’s actual position being discussed? The entry also reminds us not to become careless “fallacy spotters.” Some argument types are reasonable in the right context, and careful evaluation is more useful than simply attaching a label.

important_terms.definition: Reasoning that looks convincing but has a weakness that prevents it from properly supporting its conclusion.
A claim or set of claims used to give support for another claim.
A problem in reasoning that can be identified by an invalid logical pattern.
A problem in everyday-language reasoning whose weakness is usually explained through meaning, evidence, relevance, or context.
Using a word in two different senses while making it seem as if the meaning stayed the same.
Treating a claim as supported when it simply repeats or assumes what it is supposed to prove.
Rejecting a claim by attacking the person or situation of the speaker instead of addressing the claim’s reasons.
Claiming that one step will inevitably lead to a chain of increasingly bad results without enough support for the links.

questions_to_think_about: Why does a straw man argument make disagreement easier but less fair?
When might an expert’s opinion be useful evidence, and when might it be an appeal to irrelevant authority?
Can an argument be logically valid but still fail to teach us anything new?
Why might philosophers disagree about whether a threat is always a fallacy?
What is the difference between causing a mistake and identifying the mistake?
